Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Shoshone Field Office The largest office in the Twin Falls District, the Shoshone Field Office is located in south-central Idaho and manages approximately 1.7 million acres of public lands. It is home to the largest known density of caves within BLM, and manages nearly 40% of the Bald Mountain Ski Area in Sun Valley. In this region, BLM co-manages the Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve with the National Park Service, which features some of the best examples of recent basaltic volcanic flows on the mainland. Another unique feature to the Shoshone Field Office is Black Magic Canyon, where the Big Wood River has carved a narrow path of exquisite, swirling rock sculptures into the surrounding black basalt. The four-mile section of complex carvings and potholes is one of the best and most beautiful examples of eroded river bedrock in the United States. While recreation opportunities attract thousands of visitors to the rivers, streams, trails and ski areas each year, livestock grazing is also part of the historic fabric in this area with 215 allotments and 172 permittees. Whether your reasons for going back to school are personal or professional, several benefits of achieving a higher level of education may help you make your choice. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition Redefinition SI stands for the International System of Units, also known as the metric system. On November 16, 2018, in Versailles, France, a group of 60 countries made history. With a unanimous vote, they dramatically transformed the international system that underpins global science and trade. This single action finally realized scientists’ 150-year dream of a measurement system based entirely on unchanging fundamental properties of nature. On that day, the International System of Units, informally known as the metric system — the way in which the world measures everything from coffee to the cosmos — changed in a way that is more profound than anything since its establishment following the French Revolution. It was a turning point for humanity. READ MORE THE SI The SI — the modern metric system — has seven base units from which all other measurement units can be derived. On May 20, 2019, four of them — the kilogram, kelvin, ampere and mole — were redefined in terms of constants of nature. The remaining three — the second, meter, and candela — are already based on universal constants. Click on the SI symbols below for more information. Signs and Symptoms of Flu Aug. 26, 2024 Español About Influenza (also known as “flu”) is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It can cause mild to severe illness, and at times can lead to death. Symptoms Flu can cause mild to severe illness, and at times can lead to death. Flu symptoms usually come on suddenly. People who have flu often feel some or all of these signs and symptoms: fever* or feeling feverish/chills cough sore throat runny or stuffy nose muscle or body aches headaches fatigue (tiredness) some people may have vomiting and diarrhea, though this is more common in children than adults. *It's important to note that not everyone with flu will have a fever. Keep Reading Signs and Symptoms of Flu Flu complications Most people who get flu will recover in a few days to less than two weeks, but some people will develop complications (such as pneumonia) as a result of flu, some of which can be life-threatening and result in death. These include fever, rash, facial paralysis, an irregular heartbeat, and arthritis. How flu and COVID-19 are different Influenza (flu) and COVID-19 are both contagious respiratory illnesses, but they are caused by different viruses. COVID-19 is caused by infection with a coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) first identified in 2019. Flu is caused by infection with an influenza virus . From what we know, COVID-19 spreads more easily than flu. Efforts to maximize the proportion of people in the United States who are up to date with their COVID-19 vaccines remain critical to reducing the risk of severe COVID-19 illness and death. OSM XML is exact but verbose, OSM JSON has no comments, and Level0L is easy to type but has no grammar beyond its parser. TOML has comments, a spec and parsers in most languages, including Python’s standard library. So what would OSM data look like as TOML? I came across this question while adding an OSM tag editor to DinoData . Below, each format is compared with TOML using the examples from the OSM wiki, and the TOML versions are checked with Python’s tomllib . Level0L is the text format of the Level0 editor. DinoData reads and writes it in the OSM text view ( src/osm/level0.ts , src/osm/tags.ts ). It looks a bit like TOML : key = value lines, # comments, and headers that start a section. pages.text: Single-Family Housing Starts Using Satellite Imagery Single-Family Housing Starts Using Satellite Imagery Skip Navigation Single-Family Housing Starts Using Satellite Imagery December 19, 2024 The U.S. Census Bureau has released a new experimental data product featuring monthly single-family housing starts for the West South-Central division. For select areas of interest, Survey of Construction (SOC) data collected by field representatives have been replaced with estimates obtained from satellite imagery to demonstrate the efficacy of this data collection method. Satellite images are acquired for selected areas of interest and run through a series of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that have been trained to identify construction stages (excavation, foundation, framing, unfinished roof, and finished roof) as well as likely building type (single-family detached, single-family attached, multi-family, and non-residential). Model output is compared for consecutive months to identify new single-family residential construction starts. These starts are combined with traditional survey data collected for the remaining areas to create a hybrid estimate for the West South-Central division. This experimental data product provides a historical monthly data series for the division from July to November 2024, and we anticipate it will be updated monthly going forward. This product demonstrates a new computer-vision based approach to monthly economic measurement that can improve geographic granularity and accuracy while also reducing respondent burden. Wales' first win against the All Blacks in 73 years has provided a timely boost for everyone connected to rugby in the country during a period of significant uncertainty. Steve Tandy's side delivered the memorable performance in front of a fervent but lowest Principality Stadium crowd of 55,152 for a Wales-New Zealand match. Not too long ago Wales were mired in a world record 18-Test losing streak, while a shadow hangs over the future of regional rugby with the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) intent on cutting a team in 2028. Davies, WRU president from 2019 to 2023, believes the gutsy showing against New Zealand has lifted spirits but wants clear direction for Welsh rugby's future. "New Zealand are the barometer around the world, but there's a big question about the future and where Wales goes from here," Davies told BBC Radio Cymru. "Are the administrators within the union able to show leadership and the vision to improve the state of the game in Wales?" pages.text: Sir Tom Jones to headline Blenheim Palace Festival Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Weather Newsletters Sir Tom Jones to headline Blenheim Palace Festival 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Kemi Spence South of England BBC/Guy Levy Sir Tom Jones has been awarded with mutiple Brit Awards a Silver Clef Award and a Hitmaker Award from the US Songwriters Hall of Fame Sir Tom Jones has been announced as the 5th headliner of Oxfordshire's Blenheim Palace Festival 2027, with Nile Rodgers & CHIC joining him as special guests. The Palace in Woodstock will host 5 nights of music in June and July next year, with performances from headliners Mariah Carey , Shania Twain , Alex Warren and David Gray. Heather Carter, managing director of visitor attraction at Blenheim Palace, said it will be an "unforgettable night for fans", as "they're both true musical icons", looking ahead to a "very special evening of music." The UNESCO World Heritage site was home to the festival for the first time this year, which saw performanes from Katy Perry, Michael Bublé and Teddy Swims. Getty Images/Jo Hale The multiple GRAMMY Award-winner Nile Rodgers and CHIC performed at Blenheim Palace as part of the previous Nocturne Festival in 2025. Get our Newsletter! Dusky shark, Carcharhinus obscurus ( CC-BY-NC-ND-2.0 ) Richard Ling An app tells beachgoers in Massachusetts and Maine if a shark has entered the area. Fishermen in Delaware check their phones to avoid accidentally catching endangered Atlantic sturgeon. Dwindling American shad, once cut off from their spawning grounds by dams, are returning in droves. Each of these stories became possible in part because of tiny “acoustic telemetry” tags and a vast network of researchers deploying them along the East Coast of the U.S. With acoustic telemetry technology, each tag emits a unique, ultrasonic “ping.” Along the Eastern seaboard, thousands of electronic receivers are listening for those pings, ready to detect any tagged animal that swims within about half a kilometer. Researchers in the Atlantic Cooperative Telemetry Network , or “ACT” for short, have been tagging animals for over two decades. Now managed by the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center , the network unites scientists from over 120 organizations from Maine to North Carolina. pages.title: Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari | National Geographic
pages.description: The Dolomites are famed for their elegant ski resorts. But there’s another way to see these uniquely craggy peaks, by spending a week skiing between rifugi, spending silent, snowy nights in these remote mountain huts.
pages.text: Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari | National Geographic TRAVEL Ski the Italian Dolomites on a hut-to-hut mountain safari The Dolomites are famed for their elegant ski resorts. But there’s another way to see these uniquely craggy peaks, by spending a week skiing between rifugi , spending silent, snowy nights in these remote mountain huts. Rifugio Lagazuoi offers refuge to skiers descending the namesake peak in the Dolomites. Manaz Productions By Katilena Dartford Published April 29, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Rifugio Lagazuoi crowns the mountain. The hut’s dark timber frame stands out against the pale rock and white snow that had drifted down overnight. This isn’t just any mountain. Here in the Dolomites are echoes of endurance; of the men who fought here in 1915, during the ‘White War’ between Italy and Austria-Hungary, when up to 12 metres of snow fell, and far harsher conditions prevailed. Throughout that winter, soldiers traversed breakneck ridges, tunnelling into them to detonate explosives, reshaping the mountain — a high-altitude frontline. It’s early January and exceptionally cold, intensified by the bone-chilling history. I double up my thermals before skiing into the Hidden Valley which descends from the hut, down the northwest side of 2,835m Lagazuoi peak. “You’re standing where people lived, fought and died,” says Tim Hudson, a silver-haired Yorkshireman who co-founded specialist ski company Inspired Italy. We’ve paused on the side of the slope, not in remembrance or ritual, but simply to listen.

pages.text: Skipper Bryce sets new Scotland run record in win over UAE - BBC Sport Image source, ICC/Getty Image caption, Kathyrn Bryce is now Scotland's leading female run-scorer Published 15 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy United Arab Emirates 138-4 (20 overs): Oza 64, Hotchandani 43; Gordon 2-24 Scotland 142-3 (18.1 overs): K Bryce 51, S Bryce 43; Dharnidharka 2-22 Scotland win by seven wickets Captain Kathyrn Bryce became Scotland Women's all-time leading run scorer as she hit an unbeaten half century in a seven-wicket win over host nation United Arab Emirates at the ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy. The skipper hit seven fours on her way to 51 not out as Scotland reached 142-3 with 11 balls to spare. It takes her international run total to 3562, one more than Kari Carswell. Her sister, Sarah Bryce, made 43, batting at number three after Darcey Carter's departure in the first over. Katherine Fraser added 15, with Pippa Sproul on 16 not out. Batting first, captain Esha Oza led the way with 64 not out as UAE reached 138-4 in their 20 overs. Heena Hotchandani added 43 before she was one of two batters to be stumped by wicketkeeper Sarah Bryce from the bowling of Kirstie Gordon. Having previously beaten Papua New Guinea and lost to Sri Lanka, Scotland sit second in Group A and are assured of a place in the Super Six stage. Scotland conclude their group games against Ireland on Wednesday. pages.text: Skylar Wallace hits three home runs for AUSL Bandits Skip to Content View this post on Instagram Skylar Wallace has been crushing pitches all season long in the Athletes Unlimited Softball League. On Thursday, her power at the plate put her in the AUSL history books. The Chicago Bandits infielder became the first player in league history to homer three times in a game. She achieved the feat during the Bandits’ 15-7 victory over the Carolina Blaze. Wallace lined a two-run dinger just beyond the right-field wall in the second inning, hit a three-run homer to left-center field in the third and added a no-doubt solo shot to right in the sixth. Even when she wasn’t hitting balls out of the yard, Wallace was still doing damage at the dish. She also had a single and an RBI double during her five-hit, seven-RBI performance. Over the past two days against the Blaze, Wallace has gone 9-for-10 with four home runs, nine RBIs and nine runs scored in a pair of Bandits victories. Chicago’s win on Wednesday clinched its spot in the AUSL postseason for the second straight year.

Photograph: Anton Melik Geographical Institute Glaciers Slovenia mourns loss of glacier on its highest peak after scorching summer Extreme heat accelerated disappearance of Triglav glacier from mountain revered as a symbol of Slovenian identity Ajit Niranjan Europe environment correspondent Tue 27 Oct 2026 13.08 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 09.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The final ice patch has vanished from Slovenia’s Triglav glacier, the latest Alpine casualty of Europe’s scorching summer. The once mighty ice mass lost 93% of its surface area between 1983 and 2003, shrinking to cover less than a hectare of overheated rock, but went on to surprise researchers who feared its imminent demise, clinging on to the mountain for two more decades. In the last five years, which includes Europe’s three hottest years on record, the remaining ice has melted to a handful of isolated pockets, with the final remnant of the main body measuring just a few metres by the end of summer.
